titleStmt.title: William Henry Jarman and Amos Fenton
titleStmt.author: Barbara Minchinton

div.p: Jarman and Fenton built the adjoining terraces at 99-101 Barry St

The adjoining heritage-fronted terraces now numbered 99 [&101] Barry St were built by the builder Peter Matthews for two single men, William Henry Jarman and Amos Fenton (The Argus 11 Nov 1867 p.3). Jarman was born in London and came to Melbourne with his family in 1849 at the age of nine. His father Henry was a carpenter. Amos Fenton came to Melbourne from Launceston in 1839 with his family at the age of two (Launceston Advertiser 7 Nov 1839 p.2). His father was a hay dealer (The Age 30 Aug 1875 p.1).

Having built their adjoining houses in 1867, both men were married in 1868. Jarman married Fenton’s sister and Fenton married Susan, the daughter of a shopkeeper in Launceston (‘John Jones’, Launceston Examiner, 2 September 1880, p. 2). The in-laws grew up alongside each other for the next two decades, with the Fenton parents in Barry Street too and the Jarman parents in Bouverie Street for their later years. The Jarmans had eight children and they all lived to a good age. The Fentons had four, and lost two very young.

Before his marriage Amos Fenton invested in gold mines and worked in his father’s business at the Haymarket, which he shared with his sister Eliza’s husband for a time after their father’s death in 1875 (The Ballarat Star, 4 May 1865, p. 4; The Age, 30 Aug 1875 p.1; The Argus, 6 June 1882 p.8). In his later years Fenton became a commission agent, while William Jarman was a salesman before becoming an accountant (The Argus, 7 August 1886, p.15). Susan Fenton died at the house in Barry St in 1895, which was known then as ‘Pleasant House’, but after her death Amos moved to Kew and became a wood, coal and coke merchant (Launceston Examiner 27 Nov 1895 p. 1; Advocate, 24 May 1902, p. 3). He died there in 1908 leaving nothing for probate (The Argus, 28 October 1908, p. 1). The Jarmans left Carlton for retirement in leafy Balwyn, and spent the last years of their lives in Mont Albert Road. When Jarman died in 1927 his unmarried daughters were bequeathed the ‘double-fronted brick villa’ valued at £2500.
